sources.news_title: US Army declares success in detonation of lead-based explosives stockpile in Iowa
sources.text:
US Army declares success in detonation of lead-based explosives stockpile in Iowa
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa - The US Army conducted a controlled detonation of an ageing stockpile of lead-based explosives in rural Iowa on Nov 25, declaring the operation a success at safely destroying the unstable material while minimising toxic fallout.
Residents of the Iowa farm town of Middletown closest to the adjacent munitions depot were evacuated ahead of time as a precaution, while others hunkered down inside their homes to avoid exposure to lead dust emitted from the blast.
The Army and the US Environmental Protection Agency said emission monitors detected zero levels of airborne lead in the surrounding region immediately after the explosion.
Still, residents were told to remain indoors until officials gave the all-clear, and some expressed doubts about official reassurances.
The detonation followed days of public rancor and legal wrangling over the controversial disposal plan, which the authorities said was far safer than waiting for the deteriorating chemical drums to eventually blow up on their own.
Shortly after 9am CST, the Federal Emergency Management Agency posted a message on its X account confirming the detonation had been carried out and urging nearby residents to remain indoors for the time being.
“Following this morning’s controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa, residents within 20 miles who have not evacuated should continue to shelter in place and follow @EPA safety guidance until given the all clear by officials. FEMA has provided safe lodging to those who evacuated,” the agency wrote.
A short time later, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle declared that the “controlled, mitigated detonation,” designed to dispose of nearly 4,500 kg of highly volatile lead azide stored in 68 degrading plastic barrels, had “exceeded all expectations and was a huge success.”
“The threat of a spontaneous detonation has been eliminated,” he said on X.
‘No kickout’
In a videotaped public service message posted online afterward, Army Colonel Aaron Teller, a munitions specialist who oversaw the operation, said the demolition and the array of safety measures to muffle the blast and emissions worked.
“All of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed,” Teller said, adding there were no secondary explosions.
“There was no kickout. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Teller said.
“We reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa.”
In a local television feed from the site, recorded from a considerable distance, the sound of an explosion could be heard, and a cloud of gray smoke was seen rising into the dawn-lit sky behind a line of trees before quickly dissipating.
Public safety concerns had focused on expectations that the explosion would spew a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock beyond the detonation site at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, about 150 miles (241km) south-west of the state capital Des Moines.
The EPA reported one hour after the blast that “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region”.
The agency said it would continue taking air, soil and water samples throughout the day to compare with more than 1,200 samples collected the day before the blast.
Residents in the area expressed relief mixed with scepticism about the Government’s candor regarding emissions from the exploded chemicals.
“If you’re going to blow them up, there are going to be some particles,” said Rhonda Woodson, a former employee of the ammunition plant who lives in nearby Burlington, Iowa.
Woodson said she thought the detonation may have been “too hyped up” but also said she did not fully trust information coming from the federal government.
Still, Woodson’s neighborhood appeared deserted some three hours after the blast. “I see no animals, no kids. Nobody’s outside,” she said.
Containment measures
Government experts had stressed that the controlled detonation of the chemical stockpile was the safest way of disposing of it.
The toxic material, growing ever more unstable with the arrival of colder weather, was otherwise certain to eventually explode on its own, they said.
Experts likewise concluded that attempting to chemically neutralise or relocate the storage drums would have triggered an uncontrolled blast.
Army projections released on Nov 23 had shown that lead dust could settle on surfaces as far as 40 miles south-west of the blast site, extending through southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri.
Airborne particles could travel nearly 100 miles within eight hours, according to projections.
US and Iowa agriculture officials estimated that 350 farms might be impacted by lead fallout, based on pre-detonation forecasts.
On Nov 25, officials said various containment structures and equipment put in place at the site had evidently worked to minimise the amount of lead particulates belched from the detonation.
Those measures included earthen berms along with two towering walls stacked with tanks of water for release into the blast zone.
A misting apparatus also was employed to dampen the surrounding terrain, and fire trucks flooded the blast site with aqueous foam.
Lead azide has long been used as the chief detonating material in military ordnance. The explosive chemical was deemed largely obsolete years ago, and the Army brought unused stockpiles from bases around the country to Iowa in 2009.
The crisis in Middletown started after an inspection in March discovered a dangerous crystallisation of the storage drums and material in them, a sign that it had become dangerously unstable. REUTERS

sources.news_title: Army Detonates Bomb-Making Chemicals in Iowa: What to Know
sources.text:
The U.S. Army completed its controlled detonation of bomb-making chemicals at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 25.
The operation was carried out at 9 a.m. CT on Wednesday, resulting in two plumes of smoke. Officials said the controlled detonation successfully reduced the risks posed by the roughly 9,700 pounds of lead azide stockpiled at the facility.
Amid pushback from environmental groups, federal officials said a controlled detonation was the only safe solution in light of an increased risk of spontaneous detonations caused by rapid deterioration of the chemicals in recent months.
Here is what to know in the aftermath of the Army’s controlled explosion at the Iowa ammunition plant.
Controlled Detonation
Early indications from officials suggested that the Army’s mitigation efforts largely contained Wednesday’s explosion.
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) sensor array did not show any lead readings above 0.0 immediately following the detonation.
“The Army’s controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success. The threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated,” he wrote in an X statement.
Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command, and President Donald Trump both said the detonation and mitigation efforts exceeded expectations.
Shirley confirmed that all of the barrels of the degraded lead azide were destroyed as a result of the detonation and that there were no secondary explosions, explosive kickout, or infrastructure damage. He attributed most of the visual effects observed immediately following the detonation to more than 3,600 gallons of aqueous foam used to contain the explosion.
“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” he said.
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds also said initial feedback indicated the detonation was successful, and the state would continue to monitor data from Iowa’s emergency operations center and keep residents informed.
Reynolds had issued a disaster emergency proclamation just one day before the detonation.
Projection maps released by the Army ahead of the detonations forecasted that dust from the explosion’s plume could drift into Missouri.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said an initial analysis provided by the Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management and federal partners indicated that the mitigation efforts were successful and the explosion was “well-contained.”
Plans Following Detonation
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin told CNN on Wednesday that government officials are prepared to take “the most comprehensive measures available” to mitigate any risks caused by the explosion.
“We’re going to immediately be deploying on-the-ground manpower, soil and water sampling—any remediation efforts that are necessary in the immediate hours that follow the controlled detonation that just finished,” he said.
The EPA had 300 employees and contractors deployed on the ground before Wednesday’s detonation. They will be conducting extensive monitoring by taking water, land, and air samples and will deploy remediation efforts if needed, Zeldin said in an X statement.
The EPA also collected 1,200 samples of water, air, dust, and land before the detonation, he said.
Telle said before the controlled detonation that air quality would be monitored “throughout the operation and well into the day.”
Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Administrator Cameron Hamilton told Fox News on Wednesday that officials will also ensure there is no unexploded ordnance and the scene is safe.
“That’s a fairly routine procedure. And then from there, what you should also see if there is residual bleed off or burn off of material. We didn’t really see that in this event, which means that all the materials that were intended to be detonated, we believe that is a successful detonation,” Hamilton said.
“Sometimes you’ll see black smoke that goes up for a while; that is usually residual fuel that will burn off. We’re not seeing any of that.”
Exposure Risks
Prior to the operation, officials warned that the controlled detonation of thousands of pounds of lead azide could pose exposure risks for the public.
During a Nov. 24 news conference, Andy Nelson, director of the U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center’s Construction Engineering Research Laboratory, said the two potential risks of exposure to the chemicals were people encountering surface dust or inhaling particles in the air.
The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency has warned that there is “no safe level” of lead exposure and identified pregnant women and young children as particularly at risk.
Dr. Marjorie Peak, a consulting naturopathic physician with US BioTek Laboratories, a diagnostic lab that tests for heavy metals, environmental toxins, and other things like food sensitivities, underscored the acute and chronic effects of lead exposure in light of the controlled detonation.
Acute effects of lead poisoning include “abdominal cramps, weakness, possibly brain dysfunction, possibly even seizure or coma,” she previously told The Epoch Times.
Chronic effects of lead poisoning include heart issues, cancer, strokes, and longer-term brain issues.
Officials had recommended that all residents within Middletown and a five-mile zone southwest of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant evacuate the area prior to the controlled detonation. The evacuation was supported by FEMA.
People unable to evacuate before the detonation were advised to remain indoors and keep windows and doors closed. Those outside the evacuation zone were encouraged to shelter in place and take necessary precautions.
Despite the potential exposure risks, Tom Croci, EPA associate administrator, told reporters that a controlled and monitored detonation reduced “the risk of dust that would pose a public health problem.”

sources.text:
On Nov. 25, the U.S. Army detonated nearly five tons of unstable explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa, ending months of concern over a deteriorating military stockpile while raising new questions and concerns over possible lead contamination in surrounding communities. Residents and environmental advocates have also expressed concern that toxic particles released by the blasts could settle on farmland, potentially contaminating crops, livestock, and local water supplies.
The operation took place around 9 a.m. at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, where military explosives specialists conducted two controlled blasts to destroy approximately 9,700 pounds of lead azide, a highly sensitive chemical used in ammunition detonators.
According to the Army, all 68 barrels containing the material were destroyed without triggering additional explosions or damaging nearby infrastructure.

Initial monitoring by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) found no detectable airborne lead in surrounding areas. Federal officials issued an all-clear later on Nov. 25 (Wednesday), allowing residents to resume normal activities. However, scientists cautioned that the early results do not establish whether nearby soil, water supplies, agricultural land, or other surfaces were contaminated.
Why the army chose to detonate the chemicals

The emergency dates back to March, when inspectors found that dozens of barrels of lead azide stored in earth-covered concrete bunkers had begun to deteriorate. The chemical, commonly used to initiate explosions in military ammunition, becomes particularly dangerous when it crystallizes. Inspectors found crystalline deposits around the barrels and their lids, indicating that the material had become increasingly sensitive to friction, vibration, and temperature changes.
Army officials warned that attempting to open or transport the containers could trigger an accidental explosion. The military considered other disposal methods, including chemical neutralization and moving the material elsewhere, but found that destroying it in place presented the lowest immediate risk.
The stockpile had been transferred to Iowa from military facilities around the country in 2009 and remained in storage in case it was needed for future ammunition production. But as temperatures began falling ahead of winter, officials warned that continued delays could increase the possibility of an uncontrolled blast.
Residents evacuated over toxic dust concerns
The decision drew heavy criticism and backlash from residents and environmental organizations concerned that detonating large quantities of lead-containing explosives could release toxic particles into the atmosphere. Lead exposure can cause neurological damage and developmental problems, particularly among young children. Pregnant women are also considered especially vulnerable.
Before the detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) recommended that residents of Middletown and nearby areas within a five-mile zone southwest of the plant temporarily relocate due to the risk of exposure to toxic airborne lead particles released by the explosions.
Residents farther downwind were advised to remain indoors with windows and doors closed while the operation took place. Some schools and businesses closed ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, while homeowners took additional precautions, including sealing windows to prevent potentially contaminated dust from entering.
The Army erected concrete and sand-filled barriers around the storage bunkers and deployed water mist, foam, and other dust-suppression measures. Officials also scheduled the detonation for a period when prevailing winds were expected to carry any airborne material away from densely populated areas.
Witnesses reported two loud explosions followed by white plumes that rose above the site before dissipating.
Environmental groups challenge the plan
The detonation followed a legal dispute over whether federal authorities had adequately assessed the environmental consequences. On Nov. 19, the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter, represented by Earthjustice, challenged an emergency permit issued by the EPA.
The organizations questioned whether officials had provided sufficient public notice, conducted adequate environmental testing, and demonstrated that detonation was the safest available disposal method.
A federal court temporarily blocked the operation, but an appeals court later cleared the way for the Army to proceed. The military postponed the detonation several times, citing weather conditions and the need for additional protective measures.
Environmental advocates argued that the delays had also allowed federal authorities to improve public communication, expand monitoring, and strengthen evacuation arrangements. “Iowa and neighboring states deserve a full accounting of why the situation was allowed to get to the point of crisis,” Sarah Green, executive director of the Iowa Environmental Council, told the Associated Press.
What did the initial environmental tests find?
Before the blast, the EPA deployed approximately 300 personnel and contractors to the region and collected more than 1,200 environmental samples in hopes of establishing baseline measurements for comparison with post-detonation results. The samples included air, soil, water, and surface dust collected from communities surrounding the ammunition plant.
After the detonation, the agency reported that real-time air monitors had detected no airborne lead in the region. Army officials described the operation as successful, saying the barriers and suppression systems appeared to have contained much of the blast.
Nevertheless, researchers emphasized that air monitoring alone cannot determine whether lead particles settled on buildings, farms, playgrounds, or water sources. Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has worked on chemical disaster recovery, told the Associated Press that the initial findings were encouraging but that laboratory analysis would be necessary before health risks could be fully assessed.
He said testing could take days or weeks, with recommendations potentially varying depending on a community’s proximity to the site and its position relative to the wind. Water treatment facilities along the Mississippi and Missouri rivers are also expected to conduct additional monitoring for possible changes in lead concentrations.
For residents near Middletown, the immediate threat of an accidental explosion may have passed. But now, the next question is whether the operation left behind contamination that could affect their homes, water supplies, and farmland long after the smoke clears.

“Lead has no beneficial role in human physiology,” she said. “In fact, lead in the human body can really mess with biology.”
People who eat fresh produce already take in trace amounts of heavy metals like lead, which is widespread in soil — but detonating a “tremendous amount” of the toxic metal raises the risk of dangerous exposure, Widmer warned.

“If there is an enormous amount that is going to be contaminating the food supply, the water, the air that people are breathing in, this is very concerning,” she said.

“Lead inhalation is one of the most efficient ways that lead can be dispersed into the human body,” she said, adding that even if it’s not inhaled, it can be dispersed into the soil. “It can stay in soil, it could stay in water,” the doctor said.
“The very concerning thing is that lead can have negative effects on the human body without even showing any symptoms,” she said. “There’s still going to have to be testing. Follow-up is really key here.”

- Learning disabilities
- Attention deficits
- Growth delays
- Hearing problems
Besides breathing in the toxic lead dust dispersed through the air, fallen particles contaminating water and soil can also pose a health risk, experts say.
Those who believe they have been exposed to lead, even without showing symptoms, should visit a healthcare provider for a blood test to check for exposure and lead levels, Widmer advised.

By Zachary Stieber 
Contributing Writer 
The U.S. Army on Wednesday set off bomb-making chemicals at an Iowa facility.
Approximately 68 drums of lead azide, totaling nearly 5 tons, were detonated at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown in southeast Iowa.
“Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations,” President Donald Trump said on Truth Social shortly after the detonations.
Adam Telle, the Army’s acting secretary, said in a statement that the operation “was a huge success” and eliminated the threat of spontaneous detonation.
Lead dust was expected to be expelled southwest, potentially into Missouri, according to modeling maps released by the Army prior to the detonations.
Telle said that initial readings from Environmental Protection Agency sensors were zero.
“Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained,” Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said in a statement.
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds declared a disaster emergency ahead of the detonations and said Iowa officials were working with federal and local partners to ensure communities have the resources and information they need before, during and after the operation.
Some residents evacuated the area rather than risk exposure to dust from the exploded lead azide. Others remained indoors with doors and windows closed.
Residents who live within 20 miles who did not evacuate should continue to shelter in place until officials clear them to leave, the Federal Emergency Management Agency said.
Lead exposure has been linked to brain damage, behavioral problems and other issues, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The CDC says on its website that even low levels of lead in the blood have been linked to negative impacts on the health of children.
Military personnel had put into place a water wall and other barriers to try to absorb the impact of the blast and particulate matter it set off.
The nation’s stockpile of lead azide, historically used as explosives, was moved to the plant around 2009, according to Rob Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.
Leaving the lead azide at the plant was not an option because it can detonate spontaneously, officials told reporters at a briefing in Iowa on Tuesday. Crystallized lead azide had been accumulating on the barrels, including the lids, according to Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the 71st Explosive Ordnance Disposal Group, which prevented crews from moving them or opening the lids to treat the lead azide with a neutralizing chemical.
“There is consensus across the experts, across the country, that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance,” Telle told reporters during the briefing.
Some local residents and outside groups had expressed concern about lead dust being sent into surrounding communities. The Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council sued to try to stop the detonations. They won a temporary stay, but an appeals court ruled earlier in the week that the Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards for minimizing the dispersal of lead dust and mitigating the risks associated with potential exposure pathways.

The U.S. kept explosives more than 77 years old as a strategic reserve. Then it blew them up.

Some of the lead azide destroyed in Iowa was already deteriorating in 2009. The military had lost its domestic manufacturing capacity, and a replacement remained under development more than two decades later.
The United States military destroyed approximately 4.4 tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa on Wednesday, including material manufactured more than three-quarters of a century ago.
The Army carried out two controlled detonations shortly after 9 a.m. local time at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Witnesses reported two loud explosions and brief white plumes rising above the facility before dissipating. Military officials subsequently described the operation as successful.
The military had kept the explosives for a reason: the United States had lost its domestic manufacturing capacity for lead azide, leaving it dependent on ageing reserves while researchers struggled to develop a replacement.
Some of the material was already more than 60 years old and showing signs of deterioration when the military consolidated its supplies in Iowa in 2009. That places its manufacture before approximately 1949, around the end of the Second World War or possibly earlier.
Lead azide is a primary explosive used in detonators that initiate larger explosions in artillery shells, grenades and other military ammunition. Its sensitivity makes it useful for that purpose, but also dangerous and expensive to manufacture. Its lead content presents additional health and environmental hazards.
By the early 2000s, American manufacturers had stopped producing the compound domestically.
A September 2010 Army publication acknowledged the loss of domestic production and predicted that the military’s remaining lead azide supplies would last another three to five years.
Preserving the existing stockpile therefore served a practical purpose. The material could support ammunition production while researchers worked toward a reliable substitute.
But the Army had recognized the deterioration problem years earlier.
In a 2014 publication, the military described replacement research launched in 2004 partly because of concerns about a 40-year-old lead azide stockpile deteriorating at the Iowa facility.
The military was therefore documenting concerns about ageing lead azide more than two decades before Wednesday’s destruction.
Researchers pursued alternatives, including DBX-1, a copper-based explosive intended to perform the same function without toxic lead.
The replacement showed promising results, but qualifying it for different military applications and establishing industrial production proved a lengthy process.
In a November 2, 2026 update, the Army reported extensive successful testing of DBX-1 while acknowledging that inconsistent funding had complicated development. Full-scale pilot production was not expected until late 2027 or early 2028.
Meanwhile, the old lead azide remained in storage.
The material was kept in drums containing a stabilizing water-and-ethanol mixture and underwent periodic inspection and maintenance.
By March 2026, however, inspectors had discovered extensive crystallization. Crystals had formed around the drums’ lids and other surfaces, making the material increasingly sensitive to shock and friction.
The Army warned that even opening a container could trigger an explosion, potentially setting off neighbouring drums.
Documents examined by Iowa Public Radio revealed that the plant’s operator, American Ordnance, had sought a disposal proposal from MuniRem Environmental in September 2025, months before the emergency was publicly identified.
MuniRem proposed chemically neutralizing the explosive rather than detonating it. The company reported successful small-scale tests, and the Army initially contracted it to investigate the treatment.
But on May 8, the Army secretary selected controlled detonation instead.
MuniRem maintained that chemical treatment remained feasible. The military argued that the danger was not whether the chemicals could neutralize lead azide, but whether workers could safely introduce them into the deteriorated drums.
Officials concluded that opening or moving the containers created an unacceptable risk. They also warned that falling temperatures and the inability to replenish the stabilizing mixture made further delays dangerous.
Environmental organizations challenged the decision, questioning whether safer alternatives had been adequately considered.
A federal appeals court denied an emergency request to stop the operation on November 23, allowing the Army to proceed.
Wednesday’s detonations were carried out in two reinforced, earth-covered ammunition magazines. Authorities had installed large sand barriers, water systems and foam intended to reduce the spread of lead-containing dust.
Federal officials recommended temporarily relocating residents near the plant and arranged environmental monitoring to assess potential contamination.
Lead is toxic, particularly to children, and contamination can persist in soil and water. The Army acknowledged that the explosions would release lead-containing particles, some potentially travelling beyond the military installation.
Initial environmental monitoring showed no detectable airborne lead at four Environmental Protection Agency monitoring stations southwest of the plant during the hour after the explosions. Other measurements detected some airborne lead, while testing of soil, water and surrounding surfaces continued to assess the extent of any contamination.
The facility is approximately 800 kilometres southwest of Sarnia–Lambton. Pre-detonation modelling projected the principal airborne plume toward parts of Iowa and Missouri, with no identified threat to southwestern Ontario.
The military maintained that controlled destruction presented less danger than allowing the unstable material to remain in storage.
That explains the final decision, but leaves questions about the decades that preceded it.
The Army’s own records show that ageing explosives and the loss of domestic manufacturing capacity were recognized problems as early as 2004. Some material was already more than 60 years old and deteriorating when consolidated in 2009.
The explosives were preserved because the military considered them too important to lose. More than three-quarters of a century after some were manufactured, officials concluded they had become too dangerous to keep.

sources.news_title: US Army destroys toxic explosives amid contamination fears
sources.text:
The US Army detonated a massive cache of toxic explosives stored in a tiny Iowa farming town on Wednesday, saying the materials were too unstable to move and warning residents to shelter from a potential cloud of lead dust.
Officials said the 68 drums of lead azide — the entire US stockpile of the degraded material — were at risk of spontaneous explosion, requiring their destruction at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, where they had been stored for more than 15 years.
Extensive safety measures were put in place to curb contamination from the destruction of the nearly five tons of explosive material, and officials said the operation went well, with environmental authorities detecting no airborne lead after its conclusion.
The controlled explosion sent debris flying into the air and a large cloud of smoke over a tree line, while a New York Times reporter said the blast could be heard some 10 miles (15 kilometers) away.
“We reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and (the) extended communities throughout Iowa,” US Army Major General Eric Shirley said in a video update after the blast, terming it “tremendously successful.”
The US Environmental Protection Agency said in a statement that all of its “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region.”
The detonation of the explosives was initially scheduled for November 20 but was postponed for three days, after which US President Trump paused the operation again before ultimately allowing it to proceed.
Following the explosion, Iowa’s incoming Democratic governor Rob Sand praised “the experts on the ground who did all they could to make this detonation as safe as possible,” while saying that the “lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear.”
‘Extensive protective works’
Hakeem Jeffries, the speaker-designate of the US House of Representatives, took aim at the Trump administration, saying it “has repeatedly proven that they cannot be trusted to guard the health, safety and well-being of everyday Americans.”
“People need transparent information, not vague assurances of safety being made by a Defense Department led by a grossly incompetent secretary,” Jeffries added.
Colonel Aaron Teller, who led the explosives experts who carried out the detonation, said the last major disposal of lead azide occurred in 1977, when some 7,000 pounds of the substance were destroyed in an open-air blast in Colorado.
Teller said in that case, 75 percent of the lead particulate remained at the site even with no mitigation measures, and that steps were taken to better contain it in the Iowa detonation.
“There’s extensive protective works around those two bunkers, earthen-filled barriers that extend well above the tops of those magazines,” Teller told journalists ahead of the explosion.
There was also a vent in the protective works designed to send material released by the blast into an uninhabited area on the grounds of the ammunition plant.
Large water tanks were installed at the site to contain the explosion and keep lead particulate from entering the atmosphere, Teller said, while the Army also sought to curb the blast and the material it released by flooding the exterior of the magazines with a foam material.
The Army released two maps on Wednesday morning, one showing potential exposure to toxic lead dust in the air in an area extending more than 75 miles (120 kilometers) southwest of the blast site, and another picturing possible exposure on surfaces in a more limited area.
“Consider avoiding the highlighted area or remain indoors with windows/doors closed,” the maps said, warning that “children under six are especially vulnerable to lead exposure.”
The Army also urged a local evacuation prior to the detonation, saying the Federal Emergency Management Agency was “supporting the recommended relocation for all residents of Middletown, Iowa, and immediate surrounding impacted areas.”

sources.news_title: Army calls detonation of bomb chemicals in Iowa success after fears of toxic plume
sources.text:
The U.S. Army intentionally blew up the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives, in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday after officials said the five tons of material had degraded and were at risk of exploding uncontrollably as temperatures cooled.
The exact plan for the detonation was announced just days in advance, setting off concerns about potential health and environmental impacts from toxic dust laced with lead, as well as frustration over a lack of information.
Those in charge of the operation called it a success. All of the lead azide was successfully destroyed, Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who led the Army operation, said at a news conference two hours later. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency air monitors were reporting no lead in the air around the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown.” alt=”” />
An Associated Press reporter watched and filmed the blast, along with several other bystanders who pulled to the side of a road, less than a mile away and upwind from the site. Following two loud booms around 9 a.m. local time, a pair of wispy white plumes rolled high in the air before quickly dissipating.
Bystanders laughed and joked about the size of the blast and smoke. No one there was wearing masks or eye protection.
Burlington resident Tim Brandt said he wanted to see a big boom and feel the ground shake, but instead the detonation reminded him of the noisemakers that crack when thrown on the ground.
“It was nothing,” he told The AP. “It seemed like government put fear in a lot of people over nothing.”
Still, it’s unclear yet whether the plume carried any toxic lead toward the homes and farms in its path. Lead is a heavy metal that’s not safe at any level and is especially dangerous to children and pregnant women. The wind on Wednesday was expected to carry the plume southwest toward Missouri and away from nearby Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people along the Mississippi River.
The federal government and other researchers planned extensive environmental testing in the coming days.
President Donald Trump posted on social media that early reports showed the “Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations.”
Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle along with the Republican governors of Iowa and neighboring Missouri also said it appeared to be a success and that the explosion was well-contained.
Safety concerns and weather conditions delayed the detonation
Schools that weren’t already closed for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday canceled classes, and a gas station near the detonation site posted a note on the front door saying they’d be back open once it’s safe. Some residents sealed their windows and doors as a precaution.
The blast originally was planned for last Friday. The Army changed the detonation date three times amid public backlash and to allow more time for safety measures and favorable wind, according to court documents.
“Inaction is no longer an option,” Shirley had said.
Government officials encouraged residents within 5 miles (8 kilometers) of the site to evacuate to avoid lead dust in the air.” alt=”” />
The Army took steps to quash the plume
The Army set up additional “blast barriers” around the two bunkers where the 68 barrels of lead azide were detonated. The materials were surrounded by concrete and sand barriers two stories high.
Ballistic gels and foams were intended to absorb the lead dust, and the Army planned to douse the materials with more than 100,000 gallons of water to tamp down the plume.
A video of the site released by the Army before the detonation showed a bunker encased by an earth berm and sand-filled blocks.
Colin Wellenkamp, executive director of the Mississippi River Cities and Towns Initiative, told the AP that the Army’s measures seem to have worked in limiting the amount of lead dispersal.
“Our water treatment facilities down the Mississippi River and on the Missouri River, in particular, will be testing periodically starting in a few hours,” he said, “just to make sure that there are no detectable spikes.”
Decades-old lead azide was crystallizing, risking spontaneous detonation
The stockpile was brought to Iowa from bases around the country in 2009, according to Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The lead azide was stored in case the military needed to use them again.
During an inspection in March, staff at the ammunition plant found the chemicals had partially crystallized, making it sensitive to friction and cold temperatures and creating the risk of spontaneous detonation.
The Army assembled experts to formulate a plan, and they found that alternative solutions like thermal treatment and neutralizing the drums’ contents were not as safe as a controlled detonation.
Court gives final approval amid pushback from environmental groups
Environmental groups filed a lawsuit to halt the plan, but a court ruling on Monday put the detonation back on track. A federal appeals court found the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust.
Residents expressed a mix of concern and resignation. Some said the timing could be better, given that it is happening the day before Thanksgiving, but acknowledged it needed to be dealt with now. Others worried about the impact on water, farms, animals and their own homes.
“I don’t think lead danger goes away any time soon,” said Lucy Giehl, who lives nearby in West Burlington. “It seems someone might have thought about all of this a little sooner before it came to this.”

Army detonates unstable lead explosives at Iowa munitions plant despite community concerns
The U.S. Army detonated a stockpile of degrading explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning, following community outcry and a legal fight over concerns of a possible dust plume containing toxic lead particles spreading after the blast.
Five tons of unstable explosive material, containing the highly sensitive compound lead azide, were blown up in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, which is a small community of about 350 people, located four hours west of Chicago by car.
As scheduled, the detonation took place at 9 a.m. local time. A few loud pops rang out in livestream footage of the explosion published by The Associated Press, followed by a faint smoke cloud that rose up above the rooftop of the Armed Forces Reserve Center building that separated its cameras from the detonation site.
Fifteen minutes after it happened, the Environmental Protection Agency reported that zero lead was detected in the air by four monitoring stations in the area. Those sensors continued to show the same readings two hours later, according to the EPA.
The Army said in a follow-up social media post Wednesday evening that the Federal Emergency Management Agency had given an "all clear" around the plant. The Army also added that maps from the Pentagon's Defense Threat Reduction Agency indicated "ZERO airborne lead detection" from the detonation. FEMA said in a separate statement Wednesday night that its air monitoring results indicated there was "no detectable lead."
Army Maj. Gen. Eric P. Shirley, the commander of the operation, described the detonation as "tremendously successful" at a news conference Wednesday.
"I believe absolutely that we reduced, as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and the safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa," he said.
Rob Cekada, the director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, added that the operation went "100% as planned," with the blast driving the explosion into the ground and minimizing the amount of lead dispersed into the atmosphere, as designed.
"The explosion exceeded all expectations," a senior administration official told CBS News. "Maximum mitigation efforts achieved."
President Trump echoed that assessment in a social media post after the detonation, writing that "early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations." An Army official told CBS News the detonation went "much better than projected," while current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds called it "successful."
"We remain in close contact with authorities on the ground, while state agencies continue to monitor incoming data from the State Emergency Operations Center," Reynolds said. "We will keep Iowans informed as details become available."
The Middletown plant housed about 68 barrels or roughly 10,000 pounds of lead azide, which has been used in ammunition since World War I. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the explosives degraded over about 20 years in storage, giving way to a process called recrystallization that made the material more susceptible to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.
The Army had pushed to carry out the controlled detonation because of the public safety risks associated with the cache possibly blowing up on its own. But environmental groups and local residents attempted to block its plans, fearing the health and agricultural consequences of a toxic plume of lead dust that could disperse across the region after the blast.
The Army said it had taken steps to barricade the concrete bunkers holding the munitions and absorb the toxic dust, including with aqueous foam, which is used to extinguish fuel fires, environmental officials have said.
"Precise deployment of aqueous foam blocks, two walls of four 16,000-gallon water tanks, and gel blocks adjacent to the bunkers will absorb thermal energy and reduce airborne particulate emissions directly at the blast source," the Army said in a statement.
Officials had warned that a plume could spread over parts of southeastern Iowa and northeastern Missouri, potentially threatening homes, playgrounds, farmlands and other spaces.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said after the explosion that reports from federal and state officials in Iowa indicated it was "well-contained."
"Initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained," Kehoe said on social media.
Legal challenge questioned detonation
The detonation was postponed last week after environmental groups filed a lawsuit challenging the emergency permit the EPA had granted the Army to authorize it. The groups argued the agency had not provided residents of the area with adequate notice of its plans or evidence showing the detonation was the best course of action from a health and safety perspective.
But the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals' initial ruling blocking the detonation was lifted Monday. The court acknowledged "the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation," but ultimately found the risk of an uncontrolled explosion more harmful.
Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said at a Tuesday news conference that plans would move forward as falling temperatures caused the explosives to become more and more volatile, increasing the chances of a spontaneous explosion. Telle said the weather forecast Wednesday was "ideal to protect public health and safety across the region."
"Inaction is no longer an option," Army Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said Tuesday. "It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward."
Mr. Trump had said earlier this week that the Army would not move ahead with the detonation without the court's affirmative ruling and the approval of Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. However, Sand was not required to weigh in and hasn't officially taken office.

sources.text:
The US Army destroyed the nation’s stockpile of lead azide Wednesday morning in a controlled blast at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The plant held roughly five tons of the explosive compound, which military officials warned could detonate on its own as temperatures fell.
Video taken several miles from the plant showed two white clouds rising over the site and quickly dispersing. Before the blast, officials had urged people living within five miles of the plant to leave the area to avoid potential exposure to lead dust.
The stockpile had been in Iowa since 2009, when the military gathered supplies from bases across the country and stored them in case they were needed again, said Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Workers discovered during a routine inspection in March that the material in storage had begun to crystallize.
“Inaction is no longer an option," Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who commanded the operation, said Tuesday. Army experts had reviewed other ways to dispose of the material in the plant’s 68 barrels and concluded that destroying it on site posed the least danger.
Residents and farmers had raised concerns that the blast could spread lead dust over homes, crops, and livestock. Environmental groups challenged the emergency permit issued by the Environmental Protection Agency, arguing that residents had received too little notice and that the agency had failed to show why detonation was the safest option.
On Monday, the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit lifted its temporary order blocking the operation. The judges acknowledged “the very real risks presented by the Army’s planned detonation" but concluded that an uncontrolled explosion posed a greater danger.
The Army had originally planned to carry out the blast the previous Friday. The delay gave crews time to put additional barriers around the storage bunkers and wait for more favorable winds. Wednesday’s forecast called for a breeze toward the southwest, away from Burlington and the Mississippi River.
The EPA said it had collected more than 1,200 samples of air, soil, and water around the plant before the blast. Its air testing had detected no lead ahead of the operation. The agency said it expected a brief rise in airborne lead after the detonation and would report air-monitoring data at five-minute intervals.

sources.news_title: ‘A Toxic Nightmare’: Pentagon Blows Up Massive Stockpile of Explosive Chemicals Near Iowa Homes and Farms
sources.text:
The U.S. Army has detonated the nation’s entire stockpile of a dangerous bomb-making chemical in southeastern Iowa, unleashing enormous white plumes above an ammunition plant as nearby residents feared toxic lead dust could spread across their homes, farms, and surrounding communities.
The controlled explosion took place Wednesday morning at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, where the military destroyed approximately five tons of degraded lead azide after officials warned that the aging material could spontaneously explode as temperatures dropped.
But eliminating the explosive threat created another serious concern: What would happen to the lead dust released during the detonation, and could it endanger people and the environment beyond the blast site?
The operation triggered widespread anxiety among residents, environmental groups, and local officials, particularly because lead is a potent neurotoxin with no known safe level of exposure. Children and pregnant women are especially vulnerable.
Video footage captured from several miles away showed two enormous white plumes rolling over the detonation site before quickly dissipating. Journalists reported hearing two powerful booms at approximately 9 a.m. local time.
Despite warnings to stay indoors, some residents pulled over along nearby roads to watch the explosion from upwind of the facility.
The Environmental Protection Agency said it was monitoring air quality during and after the detonation. Its monitors around the ammunition plant did not detect airborne lead during the first 15 minutes following the blast.
That was an encouraging initial reading, but it did not resolve the broader environmental concerns. The EPA said testing would continue to assess potential lead exposure.
The precautions were significant. Schools that weren’t already closed for Thanksgiving canceled classes, a nearby gas station posted a notice saying it would reopen once officials determined it was safe, and some residents sealed their windows and doors.
President Donald Trump quickly took to social media to praise the operation, claiming early reports showed the Army’s “mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations.”
But for families living near the facility, the explosion was hardly a routine military operation. They were left waiting to learn whether the Army’s containment measures had been enough to prevent hazardous material from reaching their communities.
The detonation was originally scheduled for last Friday. The Army postponed it three times amid public backlash and concerns about weather conditions and additional safety measures, according to court documents.
The forecast for Wednesday called for a light breeze toward the southwest, with temperatures hovering around freezing. Officials expected the wind to carry the plume toward Missouri and away from Burlington, a Mississippi River city of nearly 25,000 people.
Still, hundreds of homes and farms could potentially have been in the path of airborne dust.
Government officials urged residents within five miles of the ammunition plant to evacuate to reduce the risk of exposure. At the same time, they assured the public that barriers surrounding the blast zone were designed to contain much of the material released during the explosion.
Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the Army official overseeing the operation, defended the decision to proceed.
“Inaction is no longer an option,” he said.
The Army was facing a dangerous situation: Leave the unstable chemicals in storage and risk an uncontrolled explosion, or deliberately detonate them while trying to prevent lead contamination from spreading.
For nearby residents, neither option offered much comfort.
The military’s plan relied on an elaborate containment system intended to limit the spread of lead dust.
Officials constructed additional blast barriers around the bunkers containing the 68 barrels of lead azide. The materials were surrounded by concrete and sand barriers reaching two stories high.
Ballistic gels and foams were also intended to absorb lead particles, while the Army planned to use more than 100,000 gallons of water to suppress the dust cloud.
Video released by the Army showed the bunker surrounded by an earth berm and large sand-filled barriers.
Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle urged residents not to panic, emphasizing the precautions taken to contain the explosion.
But the scale of those precautions underscores just how seriously officials were treating the potential hazards.
And while the initial air-monitoring results showed no detectable lead during the first 15 minutes, the public will need to wait for further testing to understand the full environmental impact.
The substance at the center of the operation was not ordinary ammunition waste.
Lead azide is an explosive compound used to initiate detonations in military munitions. The nation’s stockpile had been transported to the Iowa facility from military bases around the country in 2009 and stored in barrels for potential future use, according to Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.
During an inspection in March, workers discovered that the aging material had partially crystallized.
That created a dangerous problem: The crystallized lead azide had become sensitive to friction and cold temperatures, raising the risk of an uncontrolled explosion.
Army officials assembled a team of experts to evaluate possible solutions. They concluded that alternatives, including thermal treatment and chemical neutralization, presented greater safety risks than a controlled detonation.
Environmental groups sued to stop the operation, arguing that the potential consequences for nearby communities and the environment needed greater scrutiny.
But a federal appeals court ruling on Monday cleared the way for the explosion, finding that the EPA had adequately incorporated safeguards intended to minimize the dispersal of lead dust.
For people living near the ammunition plant, the explosion brought a mixture of anxiety, frustration, and resignation.
Some questioned the timing, coming just one day before Thanksgiving. Others acknowledged that officials faced a difficult situation after discovering that the deteriorating chemicals could explode without warning.
But concerns about what happens after the blast remain.
Residents worried about possible contamination affecting drinking water, farmland, livestock, and their homes. Even if the initial air-monitoring results were reassuring, the longer-term environmental impact still needed to be assessed.
“I don’t think lead danger goes away any time soon,” said Lucy Giehl, who lives nearby in West Burlington. “It seems someone might have thought about all of this a little sooner before it came to this.”
The Army may have eliminated a stockpile that officials feared could detonate uncontrollably. But that doesn’t mean the danger is over for the surrounding communities.
The immediate question now is whether the military’s safeguards worked — and whether follow-up testing will find evidence that lead dust escaped the blast zone.

Deep Dive
The compound is used as an initiating explosive in munitions, and historically has been used in detonators to set off other explosives, such as TNT.
It is sensitive to shock, heat, impact and friction, and may explode when dry. With temperature changes and time, lead azide can form unstable, larger crystals that are even more sensitive.
The decades-old lead azide supply in Iowa was crystallising, posing the risk of spontaneous detonation.

The military stopped using lead azide in the 1980s because of its hazards.

Developing: Army Detonates Degraded Lead Azide in Middletown, Iowa
The U.S. Army intentionally detonated degraded, lead-based explosive Wednesday morning in southeast Iowa.
The operation has drawn public criticism in Iowa and across the country due to concerns about the spread of lead, which is toxic, from the detonation.
The Army decided to go ahead with the blast after significantly increasing mitigation strategies and working to evacuate the area because it determined intentional detonation was the best way to get rid of the material, which was liable to detonate on its own.
The Army said it would update the public about the status of the operation by 11 a.m. at the latest.
The most recent maps from the U.S. Army showed lead particles released from the blast were likely to travel southwest of the site, as far as 100 miles over the next several hours. Dust with lead particles was expected to settle as far as 40 miles southwest of the blast site.
Residents in those areas have been advised to remain indoors, with windows and doors closed until the Army gives an all-clear. Updates can be found online. The Army is also working with the Federal Emergency Management Agency to distribute mobile notifications to people in the area.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Army have been in Middletown and surrounding communities taking samples and are slated to take samples following the detonation to determine how much lead was released by the blast.
EPA has published a dashboard with air sampling and monitoring.
EPA leader says mitigation ‘exceeded expectations’
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a live interview with CNN Wednesday morning that the initial feedback he received from the U.S. The Department of Defense was that the mitigation efforts “exceeded expectations” in containing the plume.
Zeldin said that while EPA monitors on the ground currently show no detectable lead concentrations in the surrounding area, he encourages people in the area to wait for additional feedback before going outside.
Zeldin referenced the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks on the trade center and said in that instance, EPA told people it was safe to go outside too soon.

After multiple delays amid challenges by environmental groups, the US Army has finally pulled the trigger.
On Wednesday morning, it blew up two bunkers containing 9,700 pounds of lead-laced explosives that were stored at an Army munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa, sending towering plumes of toxic metals into the air.
Footage of the blast from KWQC shows two plumes rising from the site of the explosion. It may all but confirm fears that the blast would act like a “dirty bomb,” contaminating local residences, farmland, and rivers for potentially hundreds of square miles.
President Donald Trump immediately hailed the operation as a success.
“Early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations,” he wrote on his website Truth Social just minutes after the blast.
Prior to the explosion, authorities evacuated a five mile radius and advised those within 20 miles of the blast to stay indoors to avoid exposure. But experts and environmental groups are worried about the long-lasting effects of the blast, as lead dust can settle on surfaces and pose particular danger to pregnant people and children. The toxic metal could also be absorbed by crops and harm livestock.
The controversial decision to detonate the stockpile was made after the Army discovered that the explosive material, lead azide, had become so unstable that it could blow up at any moment, making it too dangerous to move.
A small amount of lead azide is used in bombs to trigger a more powerful but stable explosive material, such as TNT. It’s highly sensitive, and can become more volatile as it ages and crystallizes.
Ultimately, the call was made to destroy the material in a controlled explosion, which would take place in the bunkers where it’s stored underground. The Army previously explored using a chemical process to neutralize the lead azide into harmless components, but it was deemed too dangerous and time-consuming.
A group of environmental groups sued the Environmental Protection Agency last week for granting the Army permission to carry out the blast. Though the Justice Department backed the Army’s authority to blow up the lead azide if there was an “immediate threat” even without approval from the EPA, a federal court postponed the operation. The issue quickly became a political hot potato — as well as a literal time bomb — with president Trump shifting responsibility for handling the dangerous explosive cache to the state’s Democratic governor-elect Rob Sand by demanding that it shouldn’t be detonated until Sand and the courts make a decision.
At present, it’s impossible to gauge the full extent of the explosion’s fallout. It will take scientists time to measure how much lead it seeded across the rural Iowa region — over three tons of it could be blasted into the atmosphere, it’s estimated — and it may be years before we appreciate how it’s affected the health of humans and wildlife nearby. For the president to declare that the mitigation efforts have “far exceeded expectations,” in other words, is almost certainly premature.

The United States Army has detonated 68 barrels of lead azide in southeastern Iowa, disregarding concerns of residents and environmental groups about the potential harms of such an explosion.
The blast occurred around 9 am Central Time. Video from local news outlets showed several plumes of smoke from the detonation, and journalists covering the event said they felt a shockwave afterward.
The Army gave little notice about the planned detonation to local residents, announcing earlier this month that it would occur on November 20. After outcry over the announcement, the Army said it would delay the blast. A lawsuit against the Army from environmental groups further delayed the detonation until a panel of judges on the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals decided earlier this week to allow it to proceed.
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator Lee Zeldin claimed the mitigation efforts for the detonation on Wednesday “exceeded expectations.” President Donald Trump made the same claim in a Truth Social post shortly after the explosion took place. However, environmental experts say it will take more time to determine whether the mitigation efforts were entirely successful, as well as the extent to which hazardous materials were released into the environment.
New York Times reporter Quinn Glabicki said he and other journalists covering the blast “saw smoke climbing several hundred feet into the air.”
“In the distance, what appeared to be debris flew into the sky,” he added.
The 68 barrels of lead azide amounted to 9,700 pounds of the hazardous bomb-making material. The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the small town of Middletown, Iowa. Previous warnings about the planned explosion suggested the toxins could spread beyond a 100-mile radius.
Winds were moving southwest at the time of the detonation, likely pushing any material that reached the atmosphere further into Iowa or potentially into parts of Missouri.
Before the blast, the Army issued a warning, writing: “All people, but especially infants, children, pregnant women, adults, and children with chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease, or dementia, should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas until further guidance is provided.”
The Army also told nearby residents that, after an “all-clear” was issued after the blast, they should “wet-wipe high-contact exterior surfaces such as patios, decks, window sills, and outdoor play equipment to safely capture and remove any settled dust.”
Lead cleanup is notoriously difficult and often requires intervention from certified professionals. There is no safe level of lead exposure.
Two hours after the detonation, the Army held an inter-agency press conference, describing the situation as a “successful operation,” with one federal official stating that the EPA determined there was a “zero-point-zero percent detection level of lead in the atmosphere.”
Beyond the federal government’s follow-ups, some scientists said they planned to do their own investigations into the aftereffects of the blast. Shannon Bartelt-Hunt, chair of the civil and environmental engineering department at the University of Nebraska, told CNN that she urged residents in the area to collect topsoil samples before the detonation took place.
“I know the Army is doing some testing, but at the same time, I don’t think the extent of the testing that probably needs to be done is something they have fully planned,” Bartelt-Hunt explained.

US Army detonates toxic explosives in Iowa despite contamination fears
Summary
The U.S. Army detonated 68 drums of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday, after officials warned of a possible explosion and lead-dust exposure. The nearly five tons of material made up the entire U.S. stockpile of the degraded explosive and had been stored there for more than 15 years. The Army used protective measures to limit contamination and urged nearby residents to leave or shelter indoors. Initial sampling reported no detection of lead.
Key Facts
- The Army said the lead azide was too unstable to move and at risk of spontaneous explosion.
- The detonation was postponed from November 20, then paused by President Donald Trump pending a court decision and approval from incoming Iowa Governor Rob Sand; a court ruling on Monday evening cleared the way.
- Colonel Aaron Teller said a 1977 open-air disposal in Colorado destroyed about 7,000 pounds of lead azide, with 75 percent of the lead particulate remaining at the site despite no mitigation measures.
- Protective measures in Iowa included earthen-filled barriers around two bunkers, a vent directing released material toward an uninhabited area, water tanks, and foam applied around the magazines.
- Army maps showed potential airborne lead-dust exposure extending more than 75 miles southwest of the site and possible surface exposure across a smaller area; the Army said children under six were especially vulnerable.
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Army detonated a massive cache of toxic explosives stored in a tiny Iowa farming town on Wednesday, saying the materials were too unstable to move to a safer area and warning residents to shelter from the blast and a potential cloud of lead dust.
Officials said the 68 drums of lead azide — the entire U.S. stockpile of the degraded material — were at risk of spontaneous explosion, requiring their destruction at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, where they had been stored for more than 15 years.
Measures were put in place to curb potential contamination from the destruction of the nearly five tons of explosive material, but the Army encouraged residents of Middletown, Iowa and other nearby areas to leave prior to the blast "out of an abundance of caution."
Locals taped up windows to guard against flying glass and were urged to stay indoors to avoid possible toxic dust.
The controled explosion sent debris flying into the air and a large cloud of smoke over a tree line, while a New York Times reporter said the blast could be heard some 10 miles (15 kilometers) away.
US President Donald Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that "early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations."
The head of the U.S. environmental agency, Lee Zeldin, said on CNN that sampling showed there was "no detection" for now of lead.
The detonation of the explosives was initially scheduled for November 20 but was postponed for three days, after which Trump paused the operation pending a court decision and approval from the state's incoming governor, Rob Sand.
The court cleared the way for the detonation in a ruling on Monday evening, while Sand said the same day that the "administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago."
'Extensive protective works'
Colonel Aaron Teller, who led the explosives experts who carried out the detonation, said the last major disposal of lead azide occurred in 1977, when some 7,000 pounds of the substance were destroyed in an open-air blast in Colorado.
Teller said in that case, 75 percent of the lead particulate remained at the site even with no mitigation measures, and that steps were taken to better contain it in the Iowa detonation.
"There's extensive protective works around those two bunkers, earthen-filled barriers that extend well above the tops of those magazines," Teller told journalists ahead of the detonation.
There was also a vent in the protective works designed to send material released by the blast into an uninhabited area on the grounds of the ammunition plant.
Large water tanks were installed at the site to contain the explosion and keep lead particulate from entering the atmosphere, Teller said, while the Army also sought to curb the blast and the material it released by flooding the exterior of the magazines with a foam material.
The Army released two maps on Wednesday, one showing potential exposure to toxic lead dust in the air in an area extending more than 75 miles (120 kilometers) southwest of the blast site, and another picturing possible exposure on surfaces in a more limited area.
"Consider avoiding the highlighted area or remain indoors with windows/doors closed," the maps said, warning that "children under six are especially vulnerable to lead exposure."
The Army also urged a local evacuation prior to the detonation, saying the Federal Emergency Management Agency was "supporting the recommended relocation for all residents of Middletown, Iowa, and immediate surrounding impacted areas."
"Evacuated individuals will be notified by phone once the all-clear is given and at that point may return home," the Army said.

sources.news_title: Army detonates Iowa explosives amid toxic lead fears
U.S. army calls detonation of bomb chemicals in Iowa a success after earlier fears of a toxic plume
sources.text: MIDDLETOWN, Iowa -- The U.S. army blew up the U.S.’ entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives, saying the first checks show Wednesday’s controlled detonation in Iowa didn’t spread toxic dust to nearby homes and farms. Earthen barriers were put up and foam and water were poured onto a pair of bunkers holding the 5 tons (4.5 tonnes) of lead azide, and officials said those measures appear to have absorbed much of the blast. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency air monitors were detecting no lead in the air around the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Still, government agencies and independent researchers plan to do extensive environmental testing for lead -- a heavy metal that’s especially dangerous to children and pregnant women -- in the weeks ahead on water sources, farms, homes and playgrounds. The U.S. army said the safest option had been detonating the stockpile right away because it was degrading and might explode uncontrollably at any time as the weather got colder. Some experts cautioned that it’s too early to know whether communities are in the clear. But Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, who led the U.S. army operation, said the risk was “reduced as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible.” Since the military announced and then delayed plans for the detonation over the past two weeks, residents and environmental groups have voiced concerns about potential health and environmental impacts and about a lack of information about what to expect. The smoke after the blasts went away in minutes An Associated Press reporter filmed the blasts from less than a mile away and upwind from the site. Following two loud booms around 9 a.m. local time, a pair of white plumes rolled high in the air before quickly dissipating. The U.S. army attributed the smoke to the foam sprayed on the bunkers to tamp down any dust. Bystanders who parked on the side of a road to watch came away unimpressed by the size of the explosion. Burlington resident Tim Brandt said he wanted to feel the ground shake, but instead the detonation reminded him of the noisemakers that crack when thrown on the ground. “It was nothing,” he told the AP. “It seemed like government put fear in a lot of people over nothing.” The U.S. army scheduled the detonation for Wednesday because the winds were blowing to the southwest and away from populated areas including Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people along the Mississippi River. The two controlled blasts destroyed all 68 barrels and didn’t set off any secondary explosions, Shirley said. Expert says more lead test results are needed U.S. President Donald Trump posted on social media that the U.S. army did a “great job.” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle along with the Republican governors of Iowa and Missouri also said it appeared to be a success and that the explosion was well-contained. However, the final results aren’t in yet, researchers said. The EPA’s air quality data was promising, said Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters. Yet he stressed that samples need to be tested in a lab to determine if people face health risks. “This should take days to weeks,” Whelton said. “But what we may see is different guidance issued to different communities based on how far they are from the detonation area and whether or not they were upwind or downwind.” Colin Wellenkamp, the executive director of the Mississippi River Cities and Towns Initiative, said water treatment facilities along the Mississippi and Missouri rivers will be testing periodically to make sure that there are no detectable spikes. Safety concerns and weather conditions delayed the detonation Government officials had encouraged residents closest to the site and in range of the plume to evacuate, and others to stay indoors. Schools not already closed for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday cancelled classes and many businesses closed. Some residents sealed their windows and doors as a precaution. Doug Seyb, a livestock farmer from Donnellson, lives far enough away that he didn’t hear or feel the explosions. But he was still concerned about the accuracy of EPA air monitors. “All of these cows are pregnant,” he said, “and we just cross our fingers that we don’t have deformed calves and stillborns.” The U.S. army took steps to quash the plume A court ruling this week put the detonation, originally planned for last Friday, back on track. The U.S. army changed the date amid public backlash and to allow more time for safety measures and favourable wind. The U.S. army set up “blast barriers,” with concrete and sand barriers two stories high. Ballistic gels, foams and water were added to absorb the dust. Environmental groups who sued to halt the detonation said Wednesday that legal action and public pressure forced the U.S. army to take more protective measures. Had the blasts happened last week as planned, many safeguards along with clearer evacuation plans and expansive monitoring wouldn’t have been in place, they said. “Iowa and neighbouring states deserve a full accounting of why the situation was allowed to get to the point of crisis,” said Sarah Green, executive director of the Iowa Environmental Council. Decades-old lead azide was crystallizing, risking spontaneous detonation The stockpile was brought to Iowa from bases around the country in 2009, according to Robert Cekada, director of the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The lead azide was stored just in case the military needed to use it again. During an inspection in March, staff at the ammunition plant found the chemicals had partially crystallized, making them sensitive to friction and cold temperatures and creating the risk of spontaneous detonation. Nearby residents felt concern and resignation Some residents said the timing could have been better, given that it was the day before Thanksgiving, but they acknowledged it needed to be dealt with now. Others worried about the potential impact down the road. “I don’t think lead danger goes away any time soon,” said Lucy Giehl, who lives nearby in West Burlington. “It seems someone might have thought about all of this a little sooner before it came to this.” ------ By Ty Oneil, John Seewer and Scott Bauer Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio, and Bauer from Madison, Wisconsin. Associated Press writers Susan Montoya Bryan in Albuquerque, New Mexico; Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut; Jessica Hill in Las Vegas; and Chris Weber in Los Angeles contributed to this report.
