US Army conducts controlled detonation of lead-based explosives stockpile in Iowa
The US government on Wednesday conducted its planned detonation of an aging stockpile of lead-based explosives at a US Army munitions depot, as residents of an adjacent tiny Iowa farm town hunkered down in their homes to avoid any toxic dust emitted from the blast.
The Environmental Protection Agency said its teams of emission monitors reported detecting zero levels of airborne lead in the surrounding region immediately after the explosion.
The detonation followed days of public rancor and legal wrangling over the controversial disposal plan, which authorities said was far safer than waiting for the deteriorating chemical drums to eventually blow up on their own.
Shortly after 9 a.m. CST, the Federal Emergency Management Agency posted a message on its X account confirming the detonation had been carried out and urging nearby residents to remain indoors for the time being.
“Following this morning’s controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa, residents within 20 miles who have not evacuated should continue ‌to shelter in place and follow @EPA safety guidance until given the all clear by officials. FEMA has provided safe lodging to those who evacuated,” the agency wrote.
A short time later, Army Secretary Aaron Telle declared that the “controlled, mitigated detonation,” designed to dispose of nearly 5 tons (4,500 kg) of highly unstable lead azide stored in 68 degrading plastic barrels, had “exceeded all expectations and was a huge success.”
“The threat of a spontaneous detonation has been eliminated,” he said on X.
One hour after the blast, EPA chief Lee Zeldin told CNN, “Real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region,” EPA said in a separate statement. “As far ‌as the blast itself, it caved inward perfectly.”
In a live ‌television feed from the site at the scheduled detonation time, the sound of an apparent explosion could be heard and a wisp of what appeared to be gray smoke was seen rising into the dawn-lit sky from beyond a line of trees before quickly dissipating.
Public safety concerns had focused on expectations that the explosion would spew a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock beyond the detonation site at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, about 150 miles southwest of the state capital Des Moines.
On ‌Tuesday, federal, state and local officials alerted residents to evacuation plans ‌and bolstered an array of measures designed to curb the fallout, while assuring the public that the operation was under control.
The EPA said it had collected more than 1,200 air, soil and water samples for comparison to further sampling to be done on Wednesday after the explosion.
‘CONTROLLED, MITIGATED DETONATION’
Experts from the Army, EPA, the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and others stressed their consensus that the controlled detonation of the lead azide stockpile was the safest option for disposing of it.
Otherwise, they said, the increasingly volatile material, growing more unstable with the arrival of colder weather, was certain to eventually explode on its own. Experts likewise concluded that any attempt to chemically neutralize or relocate the storage drums would likely trigger an uncontrolled blast.
Army projections released on Tuesday had shown that lead dust could settle on surfaces as far as 40 miles southwest of the blast site, extending through southeastern Iowa into northern Missouri. Airborne particles could travel nearly 100 miles within eight hours, according to projections.
Some residents said changing guidance over the timing of the blast and the likely path of the lead plume had left them confused and frustrated.
Farmers and ranchers worried about protecting their crops and herds. US and Iowa agriculture officials estimated that 350 farms could be impacted by lead fallout, based on the anticipated direction of the plume.
At Tuesday’s press conference, officials said they had constructed a range of containment structures and equipment they hoped would minimize the lead particulates belched from the detonation. Those measures included earthen berms along with two towering walls stacked with tanks of water for release into the blast zone.
Engineers also installed a misting apparatus to dampen the surrounding terrain and a system to flood the ‌blast site with aqueous foam to capture dust.
In the hours following Wednesday’s blast, it was not yet clear how well those measures ‌worked.
Lead azide has long been used as the chief detonating material in military ordnance. The explosive chemical was deemed largely obsolete years ago, and the Army brought unused stockpiles from bases around the country to Iowa in 2009.
During an inspection in March, officials discovered a dangerous crystallization of the storage drums and material in them, a sign that it had become dangerously unstable, spurring deliberations over the safest way to dispose of it.

sources.news_title: Some lead azide '60+ years old' when it arrived in Iowa in 2009
sources.text:
The director of the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives says experts in his agency were called in last March to evaluate the Army’s stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown.
Robert Cekada, the first ATF agent to serve as the agency’s director, said the U.S. military began using lead azide almost 100 years ago, but transitioned to other explosives about 15 years ago because lead azide is difficult to store and transport. “What we’ve learned is about in 2009 the nation’s stockpile was moved here to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. That stockpile contained approximately 10,000 pounds,” Cekada said. “Some of that lead azide was already 60+ years old.”
The lead azide in Middletown was placed in two bunkers, which the military calls magazines. It’s surrounded by sawdust inside burlap bags and stored in containers surrounded by a mixture of water and ethanol to maintain a consistent temperature of at least 50 degrees. It prevents the liquid lead azide from crystalizing. Cekada said experts confirmed this spring that the material was crystalizing and teams haven’t been able to add the water and ethanol necessary to try to stablize it.
“Just removing the lid from one of those containers could cause a detonation of that barrel and a sympathetic detonation of every barrel inside either one of those magazines,” Cekada said.
That kind of an explosion would endanger the technicians trying to maintain the lead azide, but also the surrounding community according to Cekada. He said the fluctuation of temperatures this fall could trigger more lead azide to crystalize. “The fact that we haven’t been able to add that ethanol, now portions of lead azide are exposed to the air in the barrels,” Cekada said. “…Without that ethanol mixture at the level it should be, it’s just a matter of time when we have an uncontrolled detonation. It’s not a matter of if. It’s a matter of when.”
FEMA has sent emergency alerts to cell phones in the area surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, advising evacuations within at least a five mile zone.

The Environmental Protection Agency reported that its air monitors detected no airborne lead during the first 15 minutes following the explosion. More than an hour later, the agency again reported no detectable airborne lead.
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds also described the initial response as positive, saying feedback from state experts and federal partners indicated the detonation had been successful.
Still, the potential environmental consequences haven’t been completely ruled out.
The EPA collected more than 1,200 samples of air, soil and water before the explosion and will continue testing the surrounding area. Approximately 350 farms were identified as potentially being in the projected path of the plume.

In 2009, the Pentagon moved the nation’s entire stockpile to Middletown. Some of it was already more than 60 years old and decaying, according to Robert Cekada, director of the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.
In September 2025, six months before the Pentagon says it discovered the danger, the Army sought bids for “Lead Azide Neutralization at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.”
The stockpile required regular maintenance. The lead azide is kept wet, under water mixed with ethanol so the water won’t freeze. Because ethanol evaporates, the drums were supposed to be checked every month and topped up every September.
The private company that runs the plant is responsible for those inspections. By this spring, crystals coated the outside of 58 of the 68 drums. The drums could no longer be opened, and the September 2026 top-up was not carried out, according to a sworn court declaration by Col. Aaron Teller, who commands the unit carrying out the blast.
The Army has released no inspection records.
It waited until October to tell Middletown of its plans. Communities as far as 100 miles away first learned of the danger when the Army issued an advisory on Nov. 15.
Government-owned, run for profit
American Ordnance LLC has run the plant since 1998. It is now a unit of Day & Zimmermann, a family-owned Philadelphia company that ranks among the largest private companies in the United States and the world’s top 100 arms makers.
The government owns the land, the bunkers and the factory buildings. American Ordnance runs them for profit. It competes with General Dynamics for orders under a five-year Army contract for 155 mm shells worth nearly $1 billion. The company’s profits depend on the plant turning out shells.
While the lead azide rotted, the Pentagon was expanding ammunition production at Middletown. On July 15, four months after the Pentagon says it discovered the danger, the Army broke ground on its Future Artillery Complex, designed to load 36,000 artillery shells a month.
MSM North America, a unit of the Czech arms conglomerate CSG, got the $635 million contract without competition. Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds attended. Cannons were fired in celebration. The drums stayed in the bunkers.
The Iowa plant is the Army’s main source of 155 mm artillery shells. Most were going to Ukraine, the New York Times reported in 2023. Fired across Ukraine’s farmland, the shells leave heavy metals and explosive residues poisoning the soil.
The plant also makes tank shells used by Israel. In January 2024, fragments of an M830A1 120 mm tank shell were found in the burned-out ambulance of Palestine Red Crescent paramedics Yusuf Zeino and Ahmed al-Madhoun. Israeli tank fire killed the two paramedics as they tried to reach 6-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza City. The shell’s serial number traced back to Middletown, The Nation reported.
Today’s munitions no longer use lead azide. But the Pentagon kept the stockpile for a wartime “quick draw,” Cekada said.
Now the stockpile stands in the way of ammunition production. The Army’s own Environmental Assessment judged every disposal option by whether it would allow the plant to resume production “as quickly as possible.”
Pushing back
The people downwind did not wait. On Nov. 18, residents rallied outside the Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown. They demanded that the Pentagon halt the blast and give the communities in its path time to examine the dangers and alternatives.
EPA workers spoke out against their own agency’s decision. American Federation of Government Employees Local 704 represents about 1,000 EPA workers in six Midwestern states. The union’s president, Nicole Cantello, demanded that the blast be delayed “until more protective alternatives can be fully evaluated.”
On Nov. 19, the Pentagon put off the next day’s blast after what the Associated Press described as “an outpouring of public concern.”
Late that night, the Iowa Environmental Council and the Iowa chapter of the Sierra Club won a court order putting the EPA permit on hold.
The blast was postponed three times in one week.
Everyone signs off
As the pressure mounted, Trump tried to dump responsibility for the blast on Iowa’s Democratic governor-elect, Rob Sand, who doesn’t take office until January. Trump threatened to hold Sand responsible for “any and all death or destruction.”
Trump blamed the Obama administration for the storage. But every administration since 2004, Republican and Democratic, has let the stockpile rot.
On Nov. 23, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals lifted its hold on the EPA permit. Sand, who has no authority over the Pentagon, refused the role, saying the administration should make the decision based on what its own experts had told it. Reynolds, who had celebrated the plant’s expansion in July, called the blast a “federal operation.”
Last year, the EPA weakened the standard for cleaning up lead-contaminated soil in people’s yards.
The Pentagon kept a decaying stockpile for decades because it might need it for a war. It blew up the stockpile because the plant has to keep turning out artillery shells.
The residents and EPA workers who fought to stop the blast are up against an arms industry that treats the poisoning of people and farmland, from Iowa to Ukraine, as a cost of doing business.
The next round starts when the dust settles.

sources.text:
MIDDLETOWN, IA — The U.S. Army carried out a controlled detonation of nearly five tons of deteriorating explosive material Wednesday morning at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, according to reports from the Associated Press and NBC News.
The operation was conducted to dispose of a stockpile of lead azide, an explosive compound that had become unstable during storage. The Army determined that the material posed safety risks and required disposal.
The detonation followed legal challenges over concerns about the potential release of lead particles into the environment. The Eighth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals lifted a temporary block on the operation Monday, allowing it to proceed.
The Army and other federal agencies coordinated public safety measures ahead of the detonation, including issuing guidance to residents in surrounding communities.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency is conducting environmental monitoring to assess potential impacts from the operation. Concerns have centered on possible lead contamination affecting surrounding communities and agricultural land.
The extent of any environmental contamination, potential injuries or property damage, and the status of an official all-clear had not been independently confirmed at the time of publication.
